qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Algorithms, phase two. Search and routing. This is how maps and the internet find the way.
A map is a set of places joined by roads.
A map is places joined by roads.
Each road has a cost, and a route adds its costs up.
Each road has a cost. A route adds them up.
The fewest roads is not always the cheapest. Two roads cost nine, while four roads cost eight.
The fewest roads is not always the cheapest.
There are seven routes from A to E, so we need a method.
There are 7 routes. We need a method.
We start at A. The smallest distance is settled first.
Distance from A. Settle the smallest first.
Then we check its roads. A shorter way replaces the old distance, like B dropping from four to three.
Then check its roads. A shorter way replaces the old distance.
Now we repeat. The smallest waiting distance is always final. Two more shortcuts bring D to six, and E to eight.
Repeat. The smallest waiting (tentative) distance is always final.
The green roads are the shortest routes. A to E costs eight.
The green roads are the shortest routes: A to E costs 8.
Any other way to C goes through B, which is already further away.
Any other way to C goes via B, and B is already further.
So the smallest waiting node is final.
So the smallest waiting node is final.
A negative road breaks this. B is settled at four, but going through C reaches B for only two.
A negative road can undercut a node that was settled.
So Dijkstra needs roads with no negative cost.
So Dijkstra needs roads with no negative cost.
Now the same search on a grid, where every step costs one.
Same search, on a grid: every step costs 1.
A star adds a compass. Each cell scores g, the cost so far, plus h, a guess of the distance left.
A* adds a compass: score = cost so far g + a guess h.
The guess h counts the cells to the goal, ignoring the wall.
h counts the cells to the goal, ignoring the wall.
It tries the lowest score first. That heads straight at the goal, and then round the wall.
It tries the lowest f first: straight at the goal, then round the wall.
It finds the way round the wall, at a cost of eleven.
It finds the way round the wall: cost 11.
Same grid, same wall. Dijkstra looks in every direction, and expands fifty-nine cells.
Same grid, same wall. Dijkstra looks everywhere.
A star aims at the goal, and expands only twenty cells. Both find the same cost of eleven.
A* aims at the goal and expands far fewer cells.
But its guess must never be higher than the true cost still to go.
But its guess must never be higher than the true cost left.
A guess that is too high can fool A star, and it may miss the best route.
A guess that is too high can fool A*.
Now the places are routers. Every router learns the whole map.
Routers are the places. Every router learns the whole map.
Each one runs Dijkstra, and keeps only the first hop of every route.
Each runs Dijkstra and keeps only the first hop.
A packet arrives for F. A's table says the next hop is D.
A packet for F. A's table says: next hop D.
D has its own table, and its next hop is E.
D has its own table: next hop E.
E's table says F is one hop away. Every router uses its own table.
E's table: F is one hop away. Every router uses its own table.
Now a router has no map. A sees only its neighbours, and each says how far F is.
A sees only its neighbours. Each one says how far F is.
A adds the cost of its own road to each answer. That gives eight, nine and seven.
A adds its own road cost to each answer.
It keeps the smallest total, seven, and the next hop is D.
It keeps the smallest total, and the next hop: D.
Take a line of three routers. A reaches C through B, and B reaches C directly.
A reaches C through B. B reaches C directly.
The road from B to C breaks. B trusts A's old news, and thinks C is three away.
The B to C road breaks. B hears A's old news.
Each message adds one, so the cost creeps up, round and round, until sixteen means unreachable.
The cost creeps up, one step at a time.
Same story again, with one change.
Same story again, with one change.
With poisoned reverse, A tells B that C is unreachable, because A's route goes through B.
Poisoned reverse: A says C is unreachable, because its route goes through B.
Dijkstra settles the smallest waiting node, then relaxes its roads.
A star is Dijkstra plus a compass, the cost so far plus a guess.
Routers use a table from Dijkstra, or gossip with their neighbours.
